idiom_name: none - MRI embeds short strings inside struct RString, but the representation is explicitly private; reduce and pack objects instead
alternative: Avoid the per-object cost instead of embedding storage: reuse frozen strings and Symbols, keep small records as Struct/Data members, and pack binary values with Array#pack/String#unpack or one shared buffer - MRI's embedded-string form is not addressable from Ruby code.
implementation_notes: MRI does implement the pattern internally: struct RString overlays an 'embed' member over the heap pointer for short strings, and the header explains that Ruby 'tries to be creative to abuse padding bits of struct RString for storing contents' when a string is short enough. The same header forbids relying on it: '3rd parties must not be aware that there even is more than one way to store a string. Might better be hidden', RSTRING_NOEMBED 'has to be considered read-only', and the internal structures 'change dynamically and transparently throughout of its lifetime'. Ruby-level code therefore cannot declare an inline buffer, and a C extension that inspects one is building on an unstable representation. The practical substitutes are fewer, longer-lived objects (frozen strings, Symbols, Struct/Data), packing small values into one buffer with Array#pack, and accepting one allocation per live object where it is not measurable.
code_sketch:
NAME = "eu-west-1".freeze          # one object, reused: no per-call allocation
Row  = Struct.new(:uid, :flags)    # small record; still one object per row

packed = [uid, flags].pack("Q>B")  # pack small values into one buffer
uid, flags = packed.unpack("Q>B")  # instead of N separate objects

# MRI may embed a short string inside its RString, but Ruby code
# can neither observe nor choose that layout.
pitfalls: Frozen string literals and #freeze reduce object count but change semantics (mutation raises FrozenError) and only apply to literals; interning dynamic short strings via to_sym fills a table that is never collected before Ruby 2.2-style symbol GC, and #-@ copies instead of sharing.

MRI's embedded/heap state can change during an object's life (a short string moves to the heap on growth), so any address or capacity observed through a C extension, Fiddle or ObjectSpace is invalid after the next mutation - treat them as diagnostic only.

Packing values into a String trades object overhead for encode/decode cost and loses type safety: Array#pack formats are unforgiving (endianness, width, signedness), and a wrong directive corrupts data silently rather than raising.
sources: Ruby source, include/ruby/internal/core/rstring.h - struct RString's heap/embed union, RSTRING_NOEMBED ('has to be considered read-only') and the note that '3rd parties must not be aware that there even is more than one way to store a string': https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/master/include/ruby/internal/core/rstring.h
Ruby documentation, Array#pack - 'Packs the elements into a binary sequence' (the substitute for many small objects): https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Array.html#method-i-pack
